title: Multimodal safety: image injection, content safety and PII
summary: Anything an image says can be an instruction, a leak or a harm. No single service covers prompt injection, harmful content, PII and faces, so you layer controls and treat text read from images as untrusted.
useIf: Users or documents supply images or scans that a model reads, and the system can take actions or handle personal data.
avoidIf: Images are produced and consumed only by your own trusted pipeline with no tools and no personal data.

explain.md: OWASP names **multimodal injection**: an attacker hides instructions in an image that accompanies benign text, and reliable defences are still an open research area [[r15]]. Treat any text read from an image as **untrusted input**, like a retrieved document. Three more risks follow: harmful image content, personal data inside image text, and misuse of faces. Coverage is patchy, so check each limit (verified 2026-10-13).

Hidden text works because a model reads words in an image the way it reads your prompt, so small, low-contrast or off-screen text can ride along as an instruction, and the model has no reliable way to tell your instructions from instructions embedded in the data. Harmful content, injection, personal data and faces are four different problems with four different controls. Accessibility belongs here too: give every figure a text alternative and a data table, and review generated descriptions, because vision models can misread graphs and counts [[r1]].

explain.title: Test before you claim coverage
explain.md: The docs describe Prompt Shields for prompts and documents. Whether it reads text inside images was not verified on 2026-10-13. Red-team with hidden-text images before telling anyone it is covered.

whereToUse: Customer-support assistants that read screenshots and attachments
User-generated photo and video platforms needing moderation
KYC and onboarding flows that accept ID photos
Agents with tools (email, tickets, payments) that process uploaded images
Accessibility reviews that ensure figures have text alternatives

use: Least-privilege tools and human approval for actions after reading untrusted images
Image moderation on untrusted public uploads
OCR first, then text PII redaction and injection checks
avoid: Relying on one filter to cover injection, harm and PII together
Running document PII redaction on a JPEG and assuming it was scrubbed
Identifying people from faces without registration, legal basis and a clear use case
flips: High-impact actions: add human approval and shorter tool scopes
Uploads are internal and trusted: reduce moderation, keep injection controls
Preview tolerance is zero: avoid the multimodal moderation preview and use the GA image API

pitfalls.symptom: The agent emails a report after reading an uploaded screenshot
pitfalls.cause: Instructions hidden in the image were trusted
pitfalls.fix: Treat extracted text as untrusted, keep tools least privilege and require approval for actions. Red-team with hidden-text images.

pitfalls.symptom: An ID photo passes PII redaction untouched
pitfalls.cause: Native document PII redaction does not process digital images with embedded text
pitfalls.fix: OCR the image, redact the text, or block ID uploads from the general flow.

pitfalls.symptom: A guardrail never fires on a long OCR dump
pitfalls.cause: Foundry guardrails moderate only the first 1,000 characters of text
pitfalls.fix: Chunk the text or call the text analysis API, whose default maximum is 10K characters.

scenarios.title: Public photo uploads
scenarios.situation: A community app lets anyone post photos. Moderators drown in reports. Photos are typically 2 to 6 MB from phones.
unknowns: Which categories and thresholds fit the policy?
scenarios.question: How do you moderate?

options.name: Resize to the limits, run the Content Safety image API, and queue borderline results for review
options.why: It is built for harmful image categories, and resizing handles the 4 MB limit [[r16]].
options.tradeoff: Severities come in steps of 0, 2, 4, 6 and thresholds need tuning.

options.name: Ask a general vision model whether the photo is safe
options.why: There are no calibrated severities, behaviour drifts with prompts and the call costs more.
options.tradeoff: Useful as a second opinion on borderline items.

flips.then: Consider the multimodal API, accepting preview status.

scenarios.takeaway: Public images get a dedicated harm classifier first.

scenarios.title: Support agent with tools
scenarios.situation: A support agent reads customer screenshots and can issue refunds and send emails. A customer uploads an image with tiny white text telling the agent to refund an order.
constraints: Defences are an open research area
scenarios.question: What is the primary defence?

options.name: Treat image text as untrusted, give the agent least-privilege tools, cap refunds and require approval
options.why: Reliable detection is still open research [[r15]], so limit what an injected instruction can do.
options.tradeoff: Slower flow and some manual approvals.

options.name: Rely on Prompt Shields to catch the hidden text
options.why: Whether it reads text inside images is unverified.
options.tradeoff: Valuable as one layer for text prompts and documents.

options.name: OCR the image and strip suspicious phrases
options.tradeoff: Attackers rephrase, so it cannot be the only control.

flips.then: Injection impact drops to leaking context, so focus on output controls.

scenarios.takeaway: Limit blast radius, since detection is unproven.

scenarios.title: ID photos in onboarding
scenarios.situation: A fintech accepts photos of identity cards. The team plans to run document PII redaction on the JPEGs before storing them for debugging.
unknowns: Is the image itself needed after verification?
scenarios.question: What do you do?

options.name: Do not store ID images for debugging. If text is needed, OCR it and redact the text, and keep originals under strict access and retention
options.why: Native document PII redaction does not support digital images with embedded text [[r21]].
options.tradeoff: Debugging is harder, and you build the OCR and redaction glue.

options.name: Run document PII redaction on the JPEG and store the result
options.why: Images with embedded text are unsupported, so PII stays.
options.tradeoff: The service fits .txt, .pdf (including scanned PDFs) and .docx.

options.name: Blur faces and keep the rest
options.tradeoff: Names and numbers remain in the image text.

flips.if: Only a verification result is needed
flips.then: Store the result, not the image.
Native redaction supports scanned PDFs, test it first.

scenarios.takeaway: Redact text, not files, and do not keep what you do not need.

quiz.q: A JPEG of an ID card goes through Azure Language native document PII redaction. What happens?
options: PII in the image text is redacted
It is unsupported: digital images with embedded text are not processed
The image is converted to PDF first
quiz.explain: The docs support .txt, .pdf (including scanned PDFs) and .docx, and say digital images with embedded text are not supported. OCR first, then redact the text.

quiz.q: Which controls reduce the damage of instructions hidden in an uploaded image?
quiz.explain: Limiting tools, approving actions and treating extracted text as untrusted shrink the impact of an injection. Higher detail only makes hidden text more readable to the model.

quiz.q: Match each limit to its service.

pairs.l: Digital images with embedded text unsupported

flashcards.front: How should an agent treat text it reads from an image?
flashcards.back: As untrusted input, like a retrieved document. Defences against hidden instructions are an open research area, so use least privilege and approvals.

flashcards.front: What are the Content Safety image API limits?
flashcards.back: 4 MB, 50 x 50 to 7,200 x 7,200 px, JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF or WEBP. Image severities come back as 0, 2, 4 or 6.

flashcards.front: What does native document PII redaction support?
flashcards.back: .txt, .pdf (including scanned PDFs) and .docx. Digital images with embedded text are not supported, so OCR the image first.
